name: Abdi
title: Levites and Israelites named Abdi
lifespan: c. 10th century BC (time of David), c. 8th century BC (time of Hezekiah) and c. 5th century BC (time of Ezra)
summary: The Hebrew name Abdi (עַבְדִּי), meaning 'my servant' and likely a shortened form of Obadiah ('servant of the Lord'), refers to at least three different individuals in the Old Testament. The first appears in the Levitical genealogy in 1 Chronicles as the son of Malchijah among the Merarites, and is counted among the ancestors of the temple singer Ethan, who served in the musical ministry of the sanctuary during King David's reign. The second—and most prominent—Abdi was the father of the Levite Kish from the family of Merari. Kish actively participated in the thorough cleansing of Jerusalem’s temple during King Hezekiah’s reforms in the 700s BC, a reform aimed at restoring pure worship after widespread idolatry under King Ahaz. The third person with this name was the son of Elam; he was not a Levite but an ordinary Israelite who lived after the return from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned among those who had married foreign women and, under Ezra’s guidance, committed themselves to dissolving these marriages out of faithfulness to God’s covenant. Together, these three figures illuminate central aspects of Israel’s faith history: the continuity of liturgical service across generations, the struggle for religious renewal and reform, and the challenges of maintaining religious identity amid cultural mixing.
roles: Ancestor of the temple singer Ethan

keyEvents.title: Abdi in the line of Merari
keyEvents.description: In the Levitical genealogy in 1 Chronicles, Abdi is mentioned as the son of Malluk from the branch of Levi belonging to Merari. He was one of the ancestors of the temple singer Ethan, who played an important role in the musical service of the sanctuary during King David's reign.

keyEvents.title: Father of Kish during Hezekiah's temple reform
keyEvents.description: Another Abdi from the family of Merari was the father of Kish, a Levite who actively participated in the cleansing and consecration of the temple during King Hezekiah's religious reforms. The Levites were gathered to remove all impurity from the sanctuary and restore proper worship after the decline under King Ahaz.

keyEvents.title: Abdi among those who had taken foreign wives
keyEvents.description: A third Abdi, son of Elam, is mentioned among the Israelites who had married foreign women after returning from the Babylonian exile. In line with Ezra's exhortations, these men committed to sending away their foreign wives to preserve the people's religious identity and faithfulness to God's covenant.

The earliest occurrence is found in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles, where an Abdi is mentioned as the son of Malluk in the Levitical line of the Merarites and as an ancestor of the temple singer Ethan, who served in the sanctuary during David's time. The most prominent Abdi is known as the father of Kish, a Levite from the family of Merari who played an active role in the cleansing of the temple during King Hezekiah's sweeping religious reform in the 700s BC. In this reform movement, the Levites were gathered to restore pure worship after a period of widespread idolatry under King Ahaz. A third person named Abdi, son of Elam, is mentioned among the Israelites who had taken foreign wives during Ezra's time and who committed themselves to dissolving these marriages in order to preserve the religious purity of the people after their return from the Babylonian exile.

versions.summary: The name Abdi, which in Hebrew (עַבְדִּי) means 'my servant' and is likely a shortened form of Obadiah ('servant of the Lord'), is borne by at least three different individuals in the Old Testament. The first Abdi appears in the Levitical genealogy in 1 Chronicles, where he is mentioned as the son of Malchijah in the line of Merari and as one of the ancestors of the temple singer Ethan, who served in the sanctuary during King David's reign. The second and most prominent Abdi was the father of the Levite Kish from the family of Merari. Kish was among the Levites who actively participated in the thorough cleansing of Jerusalem's temple during King Hezekiah's religious reform in the 700s BC—a reform that sought to restore pure worship after widespread idolatry under King Ahaz. The third person with this name, a son of Elam, was not a Levite but an ordinary Israelite who lived in the period following the return from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned among those who had married foreign women and who committed themselves to dissolving these marriages after Ezra's urgent exhortations regarding faithfulness to the covenant. Together, these three figures illustrate various aspects of Israel's history of faith: the continuity of liturgical service, the struggles for religious reform, and the challenges of maintaining religious identity in a multicultural context.

footnotes.text: The name Abdi (עַבְדִּי) means 'my servant' in Hebrew and is likely a shortened form of the theophoric name Obadiah (עֹבַדְיָה), which means 'servant of the Lord'. Such abbreviated name forms were common in ancient Israel and are attested on seals and ostraca from the Iron Age found in archaeological excavations.

The Merarites formed one of the three main branches of the tribe of Levi, alongside the Kohathites and Gershonites. They were responsible for transporting and maintaining the outer structures of the tabernacle, and later for various services in the temple, including musical duties.

King Hezekiah's temple reform (c. 715–686 BC) was one of the most comprehensive religious reforms in the kingdom of Judah. The Levites played a central role in cleansing the temple from idolatry that had gained ground under his predecessor Ahaz. Assyrian annals from Sennacherib confirm Hezekiah's significance as ruler, indirectly supporting the biblical account of his reforms.

The problem with foreign wives in Ezra's time (c. 458 BC) concerned the danger of religious syncretism. Ezra demanded that Israelite men who had married women from surrounding peoples dissolve these marriages to preserve the people's religious and cultural identity after returning from the Babylonian exile.

According to rabbinic tradition (Talmud Bavli, Arakhin 11a), temple singing was an essential part of worship, on par with sacrifices. The lineage of the Merarites, to which the first Abdi belonged, was connected to this liturgical musical service.

The verse numbering in 1 Chronicles chapter 6 varies between the Hebrew Masoretic text and other textual traditions. In the Hebrew text we find Abdi in 6:29, while this corresponds to 6:44 in translations that follow a different chapter division. This is important to consider when looking up passages in various textual traditions.

Archaeological finds from Tell Arad and Lachish include ostraca with personal names containing the element 'abd' (servant), confirming that the name type Abdi was widespread in ancient Judah. Such findings provide valuable context for understanding naming practices in biblical times.

The profile covers three different individuals named Abdi from three distinct periods: the united monarchy under David (c. 10th century BC), the divided monarchy under Hezekiah (c. 8th century BC), and the post-exilic period under Ezra (c. 5th century BC). The epoch designation 'divided-kingdom' reflects the most prominent of the three.
